In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of computational tools for the prediction of protein-protein interactions and their use to model the interaction networks of organisms.

the development of new approaches to the prediction of protein–protein interactions and the development of a new protein–protein interaction database, PIPs (http://www.dundee.ac.ac.uk/www-pip), that contains >34 000 predictions of high probability protein–protein interactions that are not present in the interaction databases.
the prediction of protein interactions and the development of tools to support their analysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PIPs is an excellent database of protein–protein interaction predictions in human.
the PIPs database contains predictions of > 37,000 high probability interactions in human, >34,000 of which are not reported in HPRD, OPHID, DIP or BID.
the PIPs database is a valuable resource for the study of human protein–protein interactions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PIPs contains >37 000 predictions of protein–protein interactions for human.

we have developed a method to predict interactions in human, we have applied the method to all human proteins, we have built a database to store and display the predictions and we are providing access to the data.
PIPs is a database of protein–protein interaction predictions for human.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a combination of information on expression, orthology and domain co-occurence, with post-translational modification data and subcellular location, can be used to predict protein–protein interactions that are highly likely to be true interactions and are not reported in other databases.
a Bayesian approach that combines information from a range of data sources can be used to predict protein interactions with good confidence.
the integration of multiple information sources is a valuable strategy for predicting protein–protein interactions.
